question: May Rust act as the pre-1.0 proving ground for B49 centralized wave bookkeeping / thin Node view, and what does that imply for D32?
decision: Rust may run a pre-1.0 B49 probe and, if the probes show clear performance, memory, or profiling wins without observable protocol drift, the Rust arm may land B49 before the original post-1.0 timing. The probe must compare the current per-node bookkeeping against a GraphCore/PropagationEngine-style arena/CSR/sparse-frontier design for DIRTY/INVALIDATE traversal, diamond pending resolution, rewire churn, subscriber fanout, cache locality, and retained heap. This decision changes B49 sequencing only: D32 remains locked. Other language packages remain self-contained clean-slate packages, and cross-language coupling remains the coarse wire bridge unless a separate future decision explicitly reopens D32.
rationale: B49's risk is implementation architecture and performance, not a desired protocol change. Rust is the best early proving ground because its conformance arm is already largely green and its ownership model makes arena bookkeeping pressure visible. Advancing Rust lets the project learn before 1.0 without blocking TS's D40/D41 intent-migration work. The guardrail is explicit: if the experiment changes wave ordering, ctx.depRecords semantics, describe/GraphSpec observability, or any conformance-observable behavior, it must route through design/spec before landing. The user's proposed native-to-Rust language strategy is intentionally not locked here because it would supersede D32 and needs its own design review after B49 data exists.

question: In the Rust clean-slate graph/profile slice, should profile-enabled Graph nodes register through the process default dispatcher, or should Graph own/inject the dispatcher used by its graph-owned nodes?
decision: Use graph-bound dispatcher injection, aligned with the TS shape. A Rust clean-slate Graph binds exactly one Dispatcher at construction; callers may inject one, otherwise the Graph binds the thread-local default dispatcher (D21/D26). Every graph-owned factory path (state, producer, node, derived, effect, init_node/operator) registers node fns through that bound dispatcher. Bare substrate Node constructors also default to the default dispatcher unless their own explicit dispatcher path is used. Graph profile recording toggles and reads the bound dispatcher, while profile() remains graph-scoped by summing only the Graph's registered entries (and mounted subgraph entries via each child Graph's own bound dispatcher), not dispatcher-global totals. Profiling isolation is explicit: pass a dedicated Dispatcher when a graph must not share default-dispatcher recorder state.
rationale: This is option C from design-review, corrected to preserve D21/D26's default-dispatcher semantics and align with @graphrefly/ts. The architectural lock is the ownership/injection route: graph-owned nodes must register through the Graph's bound dispatcher, and profile reads that same bound dispatcher. The isolation boundary is therefore explicit dispatcher injection, not a silent private dispatcher default. Option A's bug was not that the default dispatcher exists, but that graph-owned nodes/profile could ignore the Graph-bound dispatcher and accidentally read or write the wrong owner. Option B (filtering a wrongly-owned/default-only profile read) still leaves registration ownership wrong. The corrected option C keeps D5/R-node-thin because counters stay in the dispatcher, preserves D26's only global singleton, supports multi-tenant/sandbox isolation via explicit dedicated dispatchers, and changes no wave-protocol behavior, ctx contract, or conformance-observable ordering.

question: How should Rust source/time APIs handle timers and async without making Tokio part of the sync core?
decision: Rust async/time sources use a feature-gated injectable local async driver. Tokio is provided as an optional adapter, not a core dependency. Timer, interval, future, and stream sources run only at the source/driver boundary; the wave core remains sync and Dispatcher::invoke remains sync void. Graph/Dispatcher may carry the driver so graph-bound sources compose without per-source runtime plumbing. Missing driver reports ERROR on source activation. Time operators are compositions over higher-order plus timer; no new protocol primitive is added.
rationale: This preserves F-SYNC-CORE, D22 single-thread graph semantics, and Rust's current Rc/RefCell local graph shape while avoiding ambient Tokio LocalSet panics as the only API failure mode. An injectable driver is testable, keeps Tokio optional, and gives Rust the B53 product surface needed for source/time completeness without changing protocol behavior; D52/D47 already cover source/time and rewire composition semantics.

question: What public shape should Rust subscribe-armed time helpers timeout/buffer_time use?
decision: Rust ships timeout(&Node<T>, ms) -> Node<T> and buffer_time(&Node<T>, ms) -> Node<Vec<T>> as graph-scoped free helper constructors anchored on the source node's arena/dispatcher/local async driver. They are not ordinary Operator<T> factories and not Graph methods. They construct construction-time timer/interval deps so clocks arm on activation before first source DATA, carry real factory names for describe auto-discovery, and clean helper clocks through rewireNext/removeDep and normal deactivation. Raw time work remains confined to timer/interval sources.
rationale: TS B41 proved timeout(source, ms)/bufferTime(source, ms) need subscribe-armed helper nodes. A plain Operator cannot arm the first clock at activation with only a source dep, while Graph methods would reverse D43's generic init_node funnel and grow per-operator surface. This preserves D52/D111, R-no-raw-async, R-dispatch-all, R-node-thin, and D6/D24 per-language sugar boundaries.

question: How should Rust add storage/read-through support for B53 reactiveCascadingCache catch-up without reviving the old graphrefly-storage graph integration?
decision: Add a new clean-slate passive storage/read-through spine inside the main graphrefly Rust crate as per-language product surface. The first Rust slice may expose a storage module with typed string-key KV tiers, memory KV, optional opaque-generation versioned KV reads plus set-if-match promotion support, and a graph-agnostic tiered_read_through helper. The old graphrefly-storage crate may be mined only as implementation reference material for backend and test ideas; it must not be imported, depended on, re-exported, or used to restore its old Graph.attachSnapshotStorage/restoreSnapshot/WAL-replay graph integration. The later reactive_cascading_cache Rust factory should be a graph-layer free helper over this passive spine, returning visible value/status/events nodes from declared request/policy/invalidate deps. This decision adds no Graph storage methods, no storage-owned hydration or restore, no graph checkpoint WAL replay, no broad CAS/transactions/locks/leases capability, and no protocol message/tier/wave semantic change.
rationale: B53 requires Rust product completeness to catch up with the already-landed TS storage and reactiveCascadingCache surfaces, while D57/D82/D103 keep storage passive and separate from graph restore/hydration. D104 split the reusable passive cascading read-through mechanics from the graph-layer reactive factory, D105/D107 locked reactiveCascadingCache as a free-standing graph helper with value/status/events nodes, and D108 allows only the narrow optional versioned KV capability needed for safe promotion. Placing the new Rust surface inside the main crate keeps graphrefly-rs self-contained per D32 and avoids freezing the retired old storage crate's port-model graph integration into the clean-slate API.

layer: L6 / messaging vocabulary and explicit validation / CSP-10 B74
question: Should Rust expose TopicMessage/JsonSchema/standard-topic vocabulary and validation as public messaging API?
decision: Rust should expose TopicMessage<T>, JsonSchema, standard topic string constants, and explicit pure JSON-schema validation helpers under messaging. This is core reusable messaging/hub vocabulary, not structural TS parity and not a semantic-memory solution runtime. Validation is caller-invoked, synchronous, side-effect-free, and limited to JSON-like payloads; message buses and dynamic hubs do not automatically enforce schemas. Schema metadata, expiresAt, correlationId, and TopicMessage metadata are application facts only and do not imply protocol messages, storage durability, restore/hydration, compatibility negotiation, retention, expiration scheduling, topic authorization, or schema registry ownership. Future schema registries, compatibility policies, retention/expiration engines, and semantic-memory pattern APIs require later design review.
rationale: Messaging will underpin many GraphReFly patterns, so a passive envelope alone would force repeated follow-up patches. A C-lite API gives reusable patterns a stable message/schema vocabulary and explicit validation primitive while preserving D132/D135 graph-visible hub semantics, D158 layering, F-SYNC-CORE, R-no-imperative, and D24/D32 intent parity. Keeping validation explicit avoids hidden hub/runtime ownership and prevents schema metadata from becoming protocol, storage, or solution-layer behavior.

layer: L6 / Rust bidirectional WebSocket session driver boundary / B72
question: What Rust driver boundary should back the D133 WebSocket SessionBundle without making drivers own session lifecycle or graph state?
decision: Rust keeps WebSocket drivers graph-owned through EnvironmentDrivers. LocalWebSocketDriver::connect remains the inbound source-stream capability, send remains the one-shot outbound capability, and an optional connect_session capability returns a live LocalWebSocketSession handle for same-connection send and close. One graph-level WebSocket driver capability may serve many independent WebSocketSessionBundle instances; each bundle owns its own request, command node, inbound, lifecycle, status, errors, attempts, retry policy, and callback fencing. Bundles do not select or carry driver objects by default; if multiple runtime backends are ever needed inside one graph, routing belongs inside the graph-installed driver or an explicitly reviewed profile/key mechanism, not per-bundle hidden driver ownership.
rationale: D130 and D131 place process/network/messaging runtime capabilities in graph-owned EnvironmentDrivers, while D133 requires bidirectional transports to expose graph-visible SessionBundle ports instead of hidden side channels. Separating connect, one-shot send, and connect_session preserves existing Rust source/outbound adapter meanings, gives D133 same-connection outbound semantics, and prevents driver instances from becoming session identity. Keeping lifecycle, retry, queueing, and errors in graph-visible bundle facts preserves F-SYNC-CORE, D39 inspectability, no hidden scheduler/EventEmitter islands, and behavioral consistency with TS without requiring structural parity.

layer: L6 / Rust CSP-10 baseline application-infrastructure scope
question: In Rust CSP-10, which retained TypeScript application-infrastructure surfaces belong in the baseline graphrefly-rs product surface, and which should remain deferred as higher application/vertical layers?
decision: Rust CSP-10 baseline includes reusable graph-visible application-infrastructure primitives such as messaging, generic orchestration/readiness, work queue, CQRS/process recipes, and related status/audit/cursor/readiness/projector vocabulary when they are Rust-relevant and can be expressed as ordinary graph facts, declared deps, passive policy/data vocabulary, or graph-visible bundles. These belong below patterns/solutions and may be used by them. Rust should not defer messaging/orchestration/work_queue merely because they are above the substrate; they are part of the basic reusable GraphReFly infrastructure surface. Deferred higher-layer scope remains LLM/vector/provider runtime adapters, product-specific WorkItem/Canvas/agent semantics, ontology policy, alias/provenance repair, multi-writer conflict repair, provider-specific context adapters, and vertical solution runtimes unless a separate design review locks a narrow Rust-native shape.
rationale: B63/D125 classify messaging, orchestration, and CQRS as reusable application infrastructure rather than patterns or vertical solutions. D130-D132 lock graph-visible environment/messaging/resilience adapter shapes; D424/D432/D433 lock scheduled readiness as provider/domain-neutral orchestration; B94/B95 show workQueue readiness convergence as generic infrastructure; B67/B72/B74 already record Rust-native intent coverage for messaging, workQueue, scheduled readiness, process/CQRS recipes, and related examples. Locking this boundary prevents two opposite drifts: under-scoping Rust by excluding reusable app-infra as too application-layer, or over-scoping Rust by pulling in LLM/vector/provider/agent product layers before concrete design. No protocol, tier, message, ctx, batch, storage-restore, or cross-language conformance behavior changes.

layer: L6 / Rust EnvironmentDrivers streaming runtime boundary / B72
question: Should Rust B72 close deferred runtime-driver design with a broad RuntimeDriver abstraction or a narrower generic HTTP byte-stream capability?
decision: Rust should add a narrow graph-owned EnvironmentDrivers HTTP byte-stream capability, not a broad RuntimeDriver abstraction. The public shape is LocalHttpStreamDriver over HttpRequest to HttpStreamDriverEvent { Head, Chunk, Error, Complete }, installed through EnvironmentDrivers and implemented by optional concrete drivers such as TokioHttpStreamDriver. Typed source adapters such as from_sse may use this capability to parse protocol-specific events, while preserving existing typed LocalSseDriver compatibility as needed. The stream capability is inbound/network-only boundary work: it does not execute providers, own schedulers, mutate graph truth, expose runtime handles, create generic sinks, replace WebSocket session semantics, or merge with Dispatcher WorkerPool or wire-bridge responsibilities. All async work remains outside the sync wave core and re-enters through existing source/DeferredCtx paths. No protocol, tier, message, ctx, batch, conformance, readiness, workQueue, CQRS, or provider-runtime semantics change.
rationale: D130-D132 allow EnvironmentDrivers to grow concrete process/network/runtime drivers when product needs require them, but reject broad generic sink surfaces and require typed graph-visible facts/bundles. D137 separates EnvironmentDrivers task/runtime work from Dispatcher WorkerPool and wire bridge work. A narrow HTTP byte-stream driver closes the real Rust gap behind from_sse and future inbound streaming adapters without freezing a monolithic RuntimeDriver contract or making raw streaming a new graph authority. Keeping response head/chunk/error/complete as driver-boundary events preserves inspectable typed source nodes, testable cancellation, optional dependency footprint, and F-SYNC-CORE.

layer: L6 / Rust SSE source over HTTP stream / B72-D567
question: How should Rust from_sse use the new D567 HTTP byte-stream capability without leaving competing SSE driver authorities or creating a broad streaming API?
decision: Rust from_sse/from_sse_with_options should resolve SSE input through a typed override plus stream fallback. If EnvironmentDrivers contains a LocalSseDriver, from_sse uses that protocol-specific driver exactly as today. If no LocalSseDriver is installed but a LocalHttpStreamDriver is present, from_sse lowers SseRequest to an HTTP GET stream request, adds Accept: text/event-stream when absent, validates the response head, parses chunks into SseEvent values inside the source adapter, and emits DATA/ERROR/COMPLETE through the existing DeferredCtx source path. Official Rust concrete runtime support should implement TokioHttpStreamDriver rather than a separate TokioSseDriver. LocalSseDriver remains a typed override/test/host-parsed protocol hook, not the default concrete runtime-driver direction. The SSE parser is adapter-local implementation, not a public generic stream parser, not a provider/runtime adapter, not a retry/reconnect scheduler, and not a replacement for WebSocket session semantics. No protocol, tier, message, ctx, batch, conformance, readiness, workQueue, CQRS, or provider-runtime semantics change.
rationale: D567 locks the generic inbound HTTP byte-stream capability while preserving typed source adapters. Keeping LocalSseDriver as the first-choice explicit override avoids breaking existing host-parsed/test drivers and respects user-installed protocol-specific capability. Falling back to LocalHttpStreamDriver gives Rust a concrete runtime path for from_sse without adding TokioSseDriver or broad RuntimeDriver surface. Adapter-local parsing preserves from_sse describe/topology shape, keeps async work at the EnvironmentDrivers boundary, and prevents raw byte streams from becoming graph truth or public application semantics.

layer: L6 / Rust HTTP stream driver event lifecycle / B72-D567-D568
question: What lifecycle contract should LocalHttpStreamDriver and TokioHttpStreamDriver follow so streaming network input remains deterministic boundary material rather than driver-defined runtime semantics?
decision: LocalHttpStreamDriver stream callbacks follow a strict finite transport lifecycle: each stream invocation emits either exactly one Head event followed by zero or more Chunk events and then exactly one terminal Complete or Error event, or emits exactly one Error event before any Head when setup/request/head acquisition fails. No Chunk may precede Head, no second Head may occur, and no callback may fire after driver-delivered terminal completion or after cancel has taken effect. Driver callbacks may occur synchronously before the DriverCancel is returned, so source adapters must fence active/terminal state independently of cancel-slot installation. HTTP status, headers, redirects, TLS, transport errors, and response-body errors remain driver boundary material; typed adapters decide whether a Head is semantically acceptable for their protocol. If an adapter rejects a Head, it emits adapter ERROR facts, marks itself inactive/terminal, ignores later driver chunks, and invokes the returned cancel once available. Empty byte chunks should be skipped by drivers when possible and ignored by typed adapters when observed. The driver owns no retry, reconnect, scheduler, buffering policy beyond transport iteration, parser state, backpressure authority, domain truth, or graph mutation authority. TokioHttpStreamDriver may use reqwest streaming under a feature gate, but dependency/runtime details do not enter public graph facts beyond Head/Chunk/Error/Complete.
rationale: D567 adds a narrow HTTP byte-stream capability and D568 routes SSE through adapter-local parsing. A strict lifecycle keeps driver behavior testable and prevents each concrete runtime from inventing status, retry, parser, buffering, or scheduler semantics. Head-before-chunk lets adapters such as from_sse validate content type/status before parsing bytes, while terminal-once and cancel fencing match existing EnvironmentDrivers callback discipline. Explicitly allowing synchronous callbacks preserves existing Rust driver patterns while requiring adapters to fence semantic rejection safely. Keeping status acceptance in typed adapters preserves typed graph-visible source semantics and avoids turning LocalHttpStreamDriver into a generic application protocol authority.

layer: L6 / Rust from_sse adapter-local parser contract / B72-D568-D569
question: What SSE parsing and validation contract should Rust from_sse use when consuming LocalHttpStreamDriver chunks without making the parser a public runtime or protocol surface?
decision: Rust from_sse's HTTP-stream fallback uses an adapter-local SSE parser following the standard event-stream line model: chunks are accumulated across boundaries, UTF-8 text is decoded incrementally, CRLF/CR/LF line endings are accepted, comment lines beginning with ':' are ignored, field lines split on the first ':', a single leading space after ':' is stripped, blank lines dispatch the current event only when at least one data line is present, repeated data fields join with '\n', event sets SseEvent.event, id sets SseEvent.id, retry parses a non-negative decimal u64 into retry_ms and ignores malformed retry fields, and unknown fields are ignored. On stream Complete, an unterminated buffered event with data is dispatched before COMPLETE; unterminated partial lines without a blank dispatch are ignored unless they complete a data-bearing event according to the accumulated parser state. The HTTP-stream fallback accepts 2xx response heads with content-type text/event-stream allowing parameters such as charset; unacceptable status/content-type, invalid UTF-8, or parser overflow emits adapter ERROR and cancels/ignores the stream per D569. The parser is private to from_sse, exposes no public parser type, no generic text/event stream source, no retry/reconnect scheduling, no Last-Event-ID management, no provider/runtime authority, and no protocol/conformance behavior.
rationale: D568 keeps SSE parsing adapter-local over the D567 HTTP stream fallback, while D569 separates transport lifecycle from typed adapter semantics. Locking the parser contract prevents each implementation from choosing different event dispatch, retry, UTF-8, content-type, and terminal-flush behavior. Keeping retry as parsed data only respects D130-D132 resilience boundaries and avoids hidden reconnect scheduling. Keeping Last-Event-ID and public parser APIs out of scope avoids turning from_sse into a broader event-stream runtime or provider adapter.
